world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: 0.2.5. The post-tonic vowels of Tolomako, Akei and Vao are lost in Sakao and tonic vowels diversify as per the following table (overleaf) [p. 7]. Tolomako forms as transcribed, §0.2.3: na βu'luku 'my hair', na 'reku 'my head', na 'poe 'pig', na 'toa 'fowl', na 'ɣutu 'louse', na 'toβu 'sugar-cane', na βe'tali 'banana', na 'para 'spider', na 'oβo 'canoe'; §0.2.7: na ɣata'tia 'moon', na βu'luna 'his hair'; §0.2.8 pronouns [p. 9]: i 'nau, i 'niɣo, i 'nie; i 'ɣitse, i ka'namu, i ka'niu, i 'ɣire; i ɣitse'rua, i kanamu'rua, i kani'rua, i ɣire'rua; i ɣitse'tolu, i kanamu'tolu, i kani'tolu, i ɣire'tolu.
new_statements.citation: Guy, J.B.M. 1974. A grammar of the northern dialect of Sakao. Pacific Linguistics B-33. Canberra: Australian National University.
new_statements.locator: §0.2.3–0.2.8, pp. 7–9 (printed; PDF pp. 17–19) — comparative Tolomako/Akei/Vao/Sakao tables
new_statements.translation_language: English (transcriptions IPA-style, stress mark ' before the stressed syllable)
new_statements.rule_in_words: No prose rule is stated. In Guy's transcriptions every polysyllabic Tolomako word (c. 45 nouns and pronouns, pp. 7–9) is marked with primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the lexical word, including compound pronouns where the numeral (rua, tolu) shifts stress rightward (ɣitse'rua, kanamu'tolu); the preposed article na and the pronominal prefix i- are outside the stress domain. §0.2.5's 'post-tonic vowels' presupposes a stressed non-final vowel followed by unstressed final vowel(s). Provisional reading: fixed penultimate word stress, inferred from consistently stress-marked data, not from an explicit statement.
new_statements.exceptions: None noted; all forms shown are penult-stressed. Vowel sequences (poe, toa, nie) are treated as two syllables with stress on the first.
new_statements.domain_note: Citation forms (isolated nouns with article na, free pronouns with i-) in a comparative wordlist; Guy's Tolomako data come from Port-Olry speakers (the language is spoken on the west coast of Big Bay from Tourébiou to Malao and by part of Port-Olry). Guy also collected the Tolomako wordlist in Tryon 1976 (Lynch & Crowley 2001:49).
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the same language, tolo1255 (ISO tlm): Guy 1974 and Guy 1994 call it Tolomako (west coast of Big Bay, Tourébiou–Malao, plus Port-Olry emigrants); Codrington 1885 ('Marina', Bay of SS. Philip and James) and Ray 1926 ('language spoken in the Bay of SS. Philip and James') are the older mission-text-based names for the same Big Bay language (Lynch & Crowley 2001:49 equate them); Meyerhoff 2009 names it by the village Matantas (Glottolog lists Matantas/Panen as names of tlm). Catalog caveat: the penult reading rests on Guy's consistently stress-marked transcriptions (c. 45 forms) and his 'post-tonic vowels' wording, not on an explicit prose rule — flag the entry as data-inferred, confidence low.

sources.note: No prose rule for Tolomako, but every polysyllabic Tolomako form in the comparative tables (c. 45 words and pronouns, pp. 7–9) carries a stress mark on the PENULTIMATE syllable (na 'poe, na βu'luku, na βe'tali, na ɣata'tia, i 'nau, i ka'namu, i ɣitse'rua, i kanamu'tolu …); the article na and pronominal i- are unstressed; §0.2.5 refers to 'the post-tonic vowels of Tolomako' being lost in Sakao. Guy is the collector of the Tolomako wordlist used by Tryon 1976 (per Lynch & Crowley 2001:49).

sources.note: Tolomako appears only in the POC consonant/vowel reflex tables (pp. ~28–49) and the 292-item wordlists; the word 'stress' occurs only in footnotes on allophones of other languages ('in unstressed syllables'). No stress statement for Tolomako; wordlist forms are not stress-marked.
